speaker: NARRATOR
text: In a certain department... but it is better not to say which department. There is nothing touchier than all sorts of departments, regiments, chancelleries and, in a word, every kind of official body. Nowadays every private person takes the whole of society to be insulted in his own person. They say that quite recently a petition came in from a certain police captain, I don't remember of what town, in which he sets out clearly that the institutions of the state are going to ruin and that his sacred name is being taken quite in vain. And as proof he enclosed with the petition an enormous volume of some romantic novel in which, every ten pages, a police captain appears, in places even completely drunk. So, to avoid any unpleasantness, we had better call the department in question simply “a certain department.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So, in a certain department there served a certain clerk. A clerk not, one could say, very remarkable: short of stature, somewhat pockmarked, somewhat red-haired, even somewhat weak-sighted to look at, with a small bald patch on his forehead, wrinkles on both cheeks and a complexion of the kind called haemorrhoidal... What can one do! The Petersburg climate is to blame. As for his rank (for with us the rank must be announced before anything else), he was what is called a perpetual titular councillor, the sort at whom, as is well known, various writers have jeered and sharpened their wit to their hearts' content, having the praiseworthy habit of leaning hard on those who cannot bite back. The clerk's surname was Bashmachkin. It is plain from the name itself that it once came from “bashmak,” a shoe; but when, at what time and in what manner it came from a shoe, nothing of this is known.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Father, grandfather, even brother-in-law and absolutely all the Bashmachkins went about in boots, merely changing the soles three times a year. His name was Akaky Akakievich. Perhaps the reader will find it somewhat strange and far-fetched, but I can assure him that it was not sought out at all, and that circumstances simply fell out of themselves in such a way that no other name could possibly be given, and it happened precisely like this. Akaky Akakievich was born towards night, if my memory does not fail me, on the twenty-third of March. His late mother, a clerk's wife and a very good woman, arranged, as is proper, to have the child christened. The mother was still lying on the bed facing the door, while on her right hand stood the godfather, a most excellent man, Ivan Ivanovich Yeroshkin, who served as a head of section in the Senate, and the godmother, the wife of a police officer and a woman of rare virtues, Arina Semyonovna Belobryushkova.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The new mother was offered a choice of any of three names that she cared to pick: Mokkiy, Sossiy, or to name the child after the martyr Khozdazat.

speaker: WOMAN
text: “No,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: thought the late lady,

speaker: WOMAN
text: “those are all such names.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: To please her they opened the calendar at another place; again three names came up: Trifily, Dula and Varakhasiy.

speaker: WOMAN
text: “This is a punishment,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the old woman said.

speaker: WOMAN
text: “What names they all are! I really never heard such names. If it were Varadat or Varukh, but Trifily and Varakhasiy!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: They turned over another page, and out came Pavsikakhiy and Vakhtisiy.

speaker: WOMAN
text: “Well, I see,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the old woman,

speaker: WOMAN
text: “that it is plainly his fate. If that is so, then let him be called what his father was called. His father was Akaky, so let the son be Akaky too.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And that is how Akaky Akakievich came about. The child was christened, whereupon he wept and pulled such a face as if he had a foreboding that he would be a titular councillor. So that is how it all came about. We relate it so that the reader may see for himself that it happened entirely out of necessity and that it was quite impossible to give him another name. When and at what time he entered the department, and who appointed him, nobody could remember.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: However many directors and superiors of every kind came and went, he was seen always in one and the same place, in the same position, in the very same post, the same clerk for copying; so that afterwards people became convinced that he had evidently been born into the world already quite ready-made, in a uniform coat and with a bald patch on his head. In the department no respect was shown him at all. The porters not only did not rise from their seats when he passed, but did not even look at him, as though a mere fly had flown across the waiting room. His superiors treated him with a sort of cold despotism. Some assistant to the head of section would simply shove papers under his nose without even saying “copy this,” or “here is an interesting, pretty little case,” or any such pleasant remark, as is the custom in well-bred offices.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And he would take it, looking only at the paper, not looking at who had put it there or whether he had any right to. He took it and at once settled down to copy it. The young clerks laughed at him and made jokes about him, as far as chancellery wit would stretch; they told stories invented about him right in front of him, about his landlady, an old woman of seventy, said that she beat him, asked when their wedding would be, and scattered bits of paper on his head, calling it snow. But Akaky Akakievich did not answer a single word to this, as if there were nobody before him; it did not even affect his work: in the midst of all these annoyances he did not make a single mistake in his writing.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Only if the joke was too unbearable, when they jogged his elbow and kept him from his work, he would say:

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Leave me alone, why do you insult me?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And there was something strange in the words and in the voice in which they were spoken. There was something in it that moved one to pity, so that one young man, newly appointed, who, following the example of the others, had allowed himself to laugh at him, suddenly stopped as if pierced through, and from then on everything seemed to change before him and appear in another light. Some unnatural force pushed him away from the colleagues whom he had met, taking them for decent, polished people. And for a long time afterwards, in the midst of his merriest moments, there would appear before him the short clerk with the little bald patch on his forehead and his piercing words:

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Leave me alone, why do you insult me?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And in those piercing words other words rang out: “I am your brother.” And the poor young man covered his face with his hand, and many times in his life he shuddered afterwards, seeing how much inhumanity there is in man, how much savage coarseness is hidden in refined, educated manners, and, O God, even in the man whom the world acknowledges as noble and honourable.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It would be hard to find anywhere a man who lived so much in his work. It is not enough to say that he served zealously: no, he served with love. There, in that copying, he saw a varied and pleasant world of his own. Delight showed on his face; certain letters were his favourites, and when he reached them he was beside himself: he chuckled and winked and helped along with his lips, so that in his face you could, it seemed, read every letter that his pen was drawing. If rewards had been given in proportion to his zeal, he might, to his own astonishment, even have risen to be a state councillor; but what he earned, as his colleagues the wits put it, was a buckle for his buttonhole and piles in the small of his back. Still, one cannot say that no notice was ever taken of him.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: One director, being a kind man and wishing to reward him for his long service, ordered that he be given something more important than ordinary copying; namely, from a case that was already finished he was told to prepare some communication to another office; the whole business was only to change the heading and to change a few verbs here and there from the first person to the third. This gave him such labour that he broke into a sweat, rubbed his forehead and at last said:

speaker: AKAKY
text: “No, better give me something to copy.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: From then on they left him to copy for ever. Outside this copying, nothing seemed to exist for him. He did not think at all about his clothes: his uniform coat was not green but of some reddish, floury colour.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: His collar was narrow and low, so that his neck, though it was not long, coming out of the collar seemed extraordinarily long, like the plaster kittens with nodding heads that Russian foreigners carry about on their heads by the dozen. And something was always sticking to his coat: a bit of hay or some thread; besides, he had a special knack of arriving beneath a window just at the moment when all sorts of rubbish was being thrown out of it, and so he was forever carrying off melon and watermelon rinds and such rubbish on his hat.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Not once in his life did he pay attention to what goes on and happens every day in the street, which, as is well known, his own brother, the young clerk, always looks at, pushing the penetration of his sharp glance so far that he will notice even whose trouser strap has come unstitched at the bottom on the other side of the pavement, which always brings a sly smile to his face.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But Akaky Akakievich, if he looked at anything, saw everywhere his own neat lines written out in an even hand, and only if, from who knows where, a horse's muzzle came to rest on his shoulder and blew a whole wind into his cheek through its nostrils, only then did he notice that he was not in the middle of a line but rather in the middle of the street. Coming home, he sat down at the table at once, hurriedly slurped his cabbage soup and ate a piece of beef with onion, not noticing their taste at all, ate it all with the flies and with whatever else God happened to send. Noticing that his stomach had begun to swell, he got up from the table, took out a little bottle of ink and copied papers that he had brought home.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And if there were none of those, he would make, on purpose and for his own pleasure, a copy for himself, especially if the paper was remarkable not for the beauty of its style but for its address to some new or important person.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Even at those hours when the grey Petersburg sky quite goes out and all the official people have eaten and dined, each as he could, according to his salary and his own fancy; when everyone has rested after the department's scratching of pens, the running about, their own and other people's necessary tasks and all that a restless man sets himself of his own free will, even more than is needed; when the clerks hurry to give the remaining time over to pleasure: the livelier one dashes to the theatre; another into the street, assigning it to the study of some little hats; another spends the evening on compliments to some pretty girl, the star of a small official circle; another, and this happens most often, simply goes to see a colleague on the third or fourth floor, in two small rooms with an entrance hall or kitchen and some fashionable pretensions, a lamp or some other trifle that cost many sacrifices, renouncing of dinners and outings; in a word, even at the time when all the clerks scatter among their friends' little flats to play whist, sipping tea from glasses with kopeck rusks, drawing smoke from long pipes, telling while the cards are dealt some gossip that has drifted down from high society, which a Russian can never and under no circumstances give up, or even, when there is nothing to talk about, retelling the eternal anecdote about the commandant who was told that the tail of the horse on the Falconet monument had been cut off; in a word, even when everyone is trying to amuse himself, Akaky Akakievich gave himself up to no amusement whatever.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: No one could say that he had ever seen him at any party. When he had written his fill, he went to bed, smiling in advance at the thought of the next day: what would God send him to copy tomorrow? So flowed the peaceful life of a man who, on a salary of four hundred, knew how to be content with his lot, and it might have flowed on to a ripe old age if there were not various calamities strewn along life's road not only for titular, but even for privy, actual, court and every other kind of councillor, even for those who give no counsel to anyone and take none from anyone themselves.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: There is in Petersburg a mighty enemy of all who receive four hundred roubles a year in salary, or thereabouts. This enemy is none other than our northern frost, although they say that it is very healthy. At nine o'clock in the morning, precisely at the hour when the streets are covered with people walking to their departments, it begins to deal such strong and stinging flicks, without distinction, to all noses, that the poor clerks absolutely do not know where to put them. At this time, when even those who hold the highest posts have an ache in the forehead from the frost and tears come to their eyes, the poor titular councillors are sometimes defenceless. All their salvation lies in running, in a skimpy little overcoat, through five or six streets as fast as possible, and then stamping their feet well in the porter's lodge, until all the faculties and talents for official duties that froze on the way have thawed out.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: For some time Akaky Akakievich had begun to feel that he was being baked in a particularly sharp way in the back and shoulder, in spite of his trying to run the lawful distance as fast as he could. At last he wondered whether there might not be some sins in his overcoat. Examining it carefully at home, he discovered that in two or three places, namely on the back and the shoulders, it had become a regular piece of gauze: the cloth was so worn that it let the light through, and the lining had come apart. It must be known that Akaky Akakievich's overcoat had also served as a target of the clerks' jokes; they even took from it the noble name of overcoat and called it a dressing gown. And indeed it was of a strange construction: its collar grew smaller every year, since it went to patch the other parts. The patching did not show a tailor's skill and came out baggy and ugly.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Seeing what the matter was, Akaky Akakievich decided that the overcoat would have to be taken to Petrovich, the tailor, who lived somewhere on the fourth floor up a back staircase and who, in spite of his one crooked eye and the pockmarks all over his face, was fairly successful at mending clerks' and all other sorts of trousers and tailcoats, of course when he was sober and was not nursing some other scheme in his head. Of this tailor, naturally, there would be no need to say much, but since it is the custom that in a story the character of every person should be fully set out, there is nothing for it, bring us Petrovich here too.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At first he was called simply Grigory and was a serf of some gentleman; he began to be called Petrovich from the time he received his freedom papers and began to drink rather heavily on every holiday, at first on the great ones and then, without distinction, on all the church ones, wherever a little cross stood in the calendar. In this respect he was faithful to the ways of his grandfathers, and when quarrelling with his wife he called her a worldly woman and a German.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Since we have already mentioned the wife, two words will have to be said about her too; but unfortunately little was known about her, except perhaps that Petrovich has a wife, who even wears a cap and not a kerchief; but she could not, it seems, boast of beauty; at least, on meeting her, only the Guards soldiers peeped under her cap, twitching a moustache and giving out some peculiar sound.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Climbing the staircase that led to Petrovich, which, to do it justice, was all smeared with water and slops and thoroughly permeated with that spirituous smell that eats the eyes and is, as is well known, inseparably present on all the back staircases of Petersburg houses, climbing the staircase, Akaky Akakievich was already wondering how much Petrovich would ask, and mentally resolved not to give more than two roubles. The door was open, because the landlady, cooking some fish, had let so much smoke into the kitchen that you could not see even the cockroaches. Akaky Akakievich passed through the kitchen, not noticed even by the landlady herself, and at last entered the room, where he saw Petrovich sitting on a wide, unpainted wooden table with his legs tucked under him like a Turkish pasha. His feet, as is the custom of tailors sitting at work, were bare.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And first of all there caught the eye the big toe, very familiar to Akaky Akakievich, with a sort of mangled nail, thick and strong as a tortoise's shell. Round Petrovich's neck hung a skein of silk and thread, and on his knees lay some rag. For some three minutes already he had been trying to thread a needle, had missed, and was therefore very angry at the darkness and even at the thread itself, muttering under his breath:

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “It won't go in, the barbarian; you have worn me out, you rogue!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Akaky Akakievich was unhappy that he had come just at the moment when Petrovich was angry: he liked to order something from Petrovich when the latter was already somewhat in high spirits, or, as his wife put it, “primed with raw vodka, the one-eyed devil.” In that state Petrovich usually gave in very readily and agreed, and every time even bowed and thanked.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Afterwards, it is true, his wife would come, complaining that her husband had been drunk and so had taken the work too cheap; but you would add a ten-kopeck piece, and the thing was done. Now, however, Petrovich seemed to be sober, and therefore stern, unyielding and fond of asking the devil knows what prices. Akaky Akakievich saw this and was about to retreat, as the saying goes, but the thing was already begun. Petrovich screwed up his one eye at him very intently, and Akaky Akakievich said involuntarily:

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Good day, Petrovich!”

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “I wish you good health, sir,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Petrovich, and squinted his eye at Akaky Akakievich's hands, wishing to spy out what sort of prey he was bringing.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “I have come to you, Petrovich, about... you know...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It must be known that Akaky Akakievich expressed himself for the most part in prepositions, adverbs and, finally, such particles as have absolutely no meaning. And if the matter was very difficult, he even had the habit of not finishing his sentence at all, so that quite often, having begun his speech with the words:

speaker: AKAKY
text: “This really is quite, you know...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: then there was nothing more, and he himself forgot, thinking that he had said everything.

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “What is it, then?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Petrovich, and at the same time looked over his whole uniform coat with his single eye, from the collar to the sleeves, the back, the tails and the buttonholes, all of which was very familiar to him, because it was his own work. It is the custom with tailors; it is the first thing he does on meeting.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Well, it is like this, Petrovich... the overcoat, the cloth... you see, everywhere else it is quite sound, it has got a little dusty and looks as if it were old, but it is new, and only in one place it is a little, you know... on the back, and then on one shoulder it is a little worn through, and on this shoulder a little, you see, that's all. And not much work...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Petrovich took the dressing gown, spread it out first on the table, examined it for a long time, shook his head and reached with his hand to the window for a round snuffbox with the portrait of some general, which general exactly is not known, because the place where the face had been was poked through with a finger and then pasted over with a square scrap of paper. Having taken a pinch of snuff, Petrovich held the coat up on his hands and examined it against the light, and again shook his head. Then he turned it lining upwards and shook his head again, again took off the lid with the general pasted over with paper, and, having stuffed tobacco up his nose, closed it, put the snuffbox away and finally said:

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “No, it can't be mended: a wretched wardrobe!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At these words Akaky Akakievich's heart sank.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Why can't it, Petrovich?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said in an almost pleading, childlike voice.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “It is only that it is worn at the shoulders; surely you have some little pieces...”

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “Little pieces can be found, little pieces will turn up,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Petrovich,

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “but to sew them on is impossible: the stuff is quite rotten, touch it with a needle and there it goes creeping away.”

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Let it creep, and you put a patch on at once.”

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “But there is nothing to put a patch on, nothing for it to hold to, the support is far too weak. It is only called cloth; blow a wind and it will fly apart.”

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Well, fasten it anyhow. Really, how can it be like this!..”

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “No,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Petrovich firmly,

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “nothing can be done. It is quite a bad business. You had better, when the cold winter weather comes, make foot-wrappings of it, because stockings are not warm. The Germans invented them to take more money for themselves”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: (Petrovich liked, when the occasion arose, to take a dig at the Germans),

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “and as for an overcoat, it seems you will have to have a new one made.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At the word “new” Akaky Akakievich's eyes clouded over, and everything in the room began to swim before him. He saw clearly only the general with the paper-covered face on the lid of Petrovich's snuffbox.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “How, a new one?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said, still as if in a dream.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “I have no money for it.”

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “Yes, a new one,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Petrovich with barbarous calm.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Well, and if I had to have a new one, how would it, you know...”

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “That is, what it will cost?”

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Yes.”

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “Well, you'll have to lay out a hundred and fifty, and a bit more,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Petrovich, and pressed his lips together meaningfully. He was very fond of strong effects, fond of suddenly bewildering a man completely and then glancing sidelong to see what sort of face the bewildered man would make after such words.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “A hundred and fifty roubles for an overcoat!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried poor Akaky Akakievich, cried perhaps for the first time in his life, for he had always been distinguished by the quietness of his voice.

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “Yes, sir,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Petrovich,

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “and what an overcoat, too. If you put marten on the collar and add a hood with a silk lining, it will run to two hundred.”

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Petrovich, please,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Akaky Akakievich in a pleading voice, not hearing and not trying to hear the words Petrovich said and all his effects,

speaker: AKAKY
text: “mend it somehow, so that it will serve a little longer.”

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “No, that won't do: it would be killing the work and wasting money,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Petrovich, and after such words Akaky Akakievich went out utterly crushed. And Petrovich, after he had gone, stood a long time with his lips meaningfully pressed together, not taking up his work, pleased that he had neither lowered himself nor betrayed the tailor's art.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Out in the street, Akaky Akakievich was as in a dream.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “So that is how the matter stands,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said to himself.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “I really never thought that it would turn out like that...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: and then, after some silence, he added:

speaker: AKAKY
text: “So that's how it is! This is what has come of it at last, and I really could not have supposed that it would be so.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: After this followed another long silence, after which he said:

speaker: AKAKY
text: “So that's how! It really is something quite unexpected, you know... I never could have... what a circumstance!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Having said this, instead of going home, he went in the quite opposite direction, without suspecting it. On the way a chimney sweep brushed against him with his whole dirty side and blackened his whole shoulder; a whole hatful of lime fell on him from the top of a house being built.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He noticed none of this, and only afterwards, when he bumped into a watchman who, having set his halberd beside him, was shaking some snuff out of a horn onto his calloused fist, only then did he come round a little, and only because the watchman said:

speaker: MINOR
text: “What are you shoving into my very face for, haven't you got the pavement?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: This made him look round and turn homewards. Only here did he begin to collect his thoughts, saw his position in a clear and true light, began to talk with himself no longer in fragments but reasonably and frankly, as with a sensible friend with whom one can discuss the most heartfelt and intimate matter.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Well, no,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Akaky Akakievich,

speaker: AKAKY
text: “it is no use talking to Petrovich now: he is, you know... his wife must have given him a beating. But I had better come to him on Sunday morning: after Saturday night he will be squinting and sleepy, so he will need something to put him right, and his wife will not give him money, and at that moment I will slip him a ten-kopeck piece, you know, into his hand, and he will be more agreeable, and the overcoat then, you know...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So reasoned Akaky Akakievich with himself, took heart, waited for the first Sunday, and, seeing from afar that Petrovich's wife had gone out of the house somewhere, went straight to him. Petrovich was indeed squinting badly after Saturday, held his head towards the floor and was quite sleepy; but for all that, as soon as he learned what the matter was, it was as if the devil had given him a push.

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “Impossible,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said.

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “Be so good as to order a new one.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Akaky Akakievich slipped the ten-kopeck piece into his hand right then.

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “Thank you, sir, I'll fortify myself a little to your health,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Petrovich,

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “and as for the overcoat, don't trouble yourself: it is good for nothing at all. I shall make you a new overcoat that is a glory, we'll stand on that.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Akaky Akakievich tried once more about mending, but Petrovich did not hear and said:

speaker: PETROVICH
text: “A new one I shall certainly sew for you, you may rely on that, we shall put in the effort. We could even, as the fashion has come in, have the collar fasten with silver clasps under appliqué.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It was then that Akaky Akakievich saw that he could not manage without a new overcoat, and his spirits sank completely. How, indeed, and with what money could it be made? Of course, he could partly rely on the bonus due at the holiday, but that money had long since been allotted and distributed in advance. He needed to get new trousers, to pay the cobbler an old debt for putting new tops on old boot-legs, and he had to order three shirts from a seamstress, and a couple of those items of linen which it is improper to name in print; in a word, all the money had absolutely to be spent, and even if the director were so gracious as to fix, instead of forty roubles' bonus, forty-five or fifty, still there would remain some trifling sum, which in the overcoat fund would be a drop in the ocean.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Although, of course, he knew that Petrovich was subject to whims of suddenly demanding the devil knows what exorbitant price, so that sometimes even his wife could not help crying out:

speaker: WOMAN
text: “What are you doing, have you gone mad, you fool! Another time he will take work for nothing, and now the devil has seized him to ask a price that he is not worth himself.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Although, of course, he knew that Petrovich would undertake it even for eighty roubles; yet still, where was he to get these eighty roubles? Half he could find: half would turn up; perhaps even a little more; but where to get the other half?.. But first the reader must learn where the first half came from. Akaky Akakievich had the habit, out of every rouble he spent, of putting aside a groat into a small box, locked with a key, with a slit cut in the lid for dropping the money in.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At the end of every half-year he would go over the copper that had accumulated and exchange it for small silver. He had gone on like this since long ago, and so over the course of several years the sum accumulated proved to be more than forty roubles. So half was in his hands; but where to get the other half? Where to get the other forty roubles?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Akaky Akakievich thought and thought and decided that he would have to reduce his ordinary expenses, at least for the space of one year: banish the use of tea in the evenings, not light a candle in the evenings, and if there was something he needed to do, go to the landlady's room and work by her candle; walking along the streets, step as lightly and carefully as possible on the stones and flagstones, almost on tiptoe, so as not to wear out the soles too soon; give his linen to the laundress as seldom as possible, and, so that it should not get worn, take it off every time he came home and stay in only a dressing gown of demi-cotton, very old, and spared even by time itself.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It must be said in truth that at first it was somewhat hard for him to get used to such restrictions, but afterwards somehow he grew used to them and it went well; he even learned quite to go hungry in the evenings; but then he fed spiritually, carrying in his thoughts the eternal idea of the future overcoat. From this time his very existence became somehow fuller, as if he had married, as if some other person were present with him, as if he were not alone, but some pleasant companion of life had agreed to walk the road of life together with him, and this companion was none other than that same overcoat, on thick wadding, on a strong lining that would never wear out. He became somehow livelier, even firmer in character, like a man who has already determined and set himself a goal.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: From his face and his actions doubt disappeared of itself, and hesitation, in a word all wavering and indefinite traits. Fire sometimes showed in his eyes; in his head even the boldest and most daring thoughts flashed: should he not really put marten on the collar? Reflections about this nearly made him absent-minded. Once, while copying a paper, he almost made a mistake, so that he nearly cried out aloud,

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Oh!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: and crossed himself. Every month he called on Petrovich at least once to talk about the overcoat, where it was best to buy cloth, and of what colour, and at what price, and though somewhat anxious, he always went home content, reflecting that the time must come at last when all this would be bought and when the overcoat would be made. The matter went even faster than he expected.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Contrary to all expectation, the director assigned Akaky Akakievich not forty or forty-five, but a whole sixty roubles: whether he had a presentiment that Akaky Akakievich needed an overcoat, or it simply happened so, but in this way he found himself with twenty roubles extra. This circumstance hastened the course of events. Another two or three months of slight hunger, and Akaky Akakievich had collected just about eighty roubles. His heart, generally very calm, began to beat. On the very first day he went with Petrovich to the shops. They bought very good cloth, and no wonder, because they had been thinking about it for half a year already and hardly a month passed without their going into the shops to compare prices; but Petrovich himself said that there was no better cloth to be had.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: For the lining they chose calico, but of such a good, thick sort that, in Petrovich's words, it was even better than silk and even looked handsomer and glossier. They did not buy marten, because it was really dear, and instead chose cat, the best that could be found in the shop, cat which at a distance could always be taken for marten. Petrovich spent altogether two weeks over the overcoat, because there was a great deal of quilting, otherwise it would have been ready sooner. For the work Petrovich took twelve roubles; less was quite impossible: everything was sewn on silk, with a double fine seam, and over every seam Petrovich afterwards went with his own teeth, pressing various patterns into it. It was... hard to say on precisely which day, but probably on the most solemn day in Akaky Akakievich's life, when Petrovich finally brought the overcoat.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He brought it in the morning, just before the time when one had to go to the department. At no other time would the overcoat have come so opportunely, because rather hard frosts were already beginning and seemed to threaten to grow still stronger. Petrovich appeared with the overcoat as befits a good tailor. In his face there showed an expression so significant as Akaky Akakievich had never yet seen. He seemed to feel fully that he had done no small thing and had suddenly displayed in himself the abyss that divides tailors who merely put in linings and do repairs from those who sew new. He took the overcoat out of the handkerchief in which he had brought it; the handkerchief was fresh from the laundress; he folded it up afterwards and put it in his pocket for use.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Having taken out the overcoat, he looked very proudly, and, holding it in both hands, threw it very deftly over Akaky Akakievich's shoulders; then he pulled it and smoothed it down at the back with his hand; then he draped it on Akaky Akakievich somewhat loosely open. Akaky Akakievich, as a man of years, wanted to try the sleeves; Petrovich helped him put on the sleeves too, and it turned out that it was good in the sleeves too. In a word, the overcoat proved to fit quite and exactly. Petrovich did not fail on this occasion to say that he had done it so cheaply only because he lived without a signboard in a small street and had known Akaky Akakievich for a long time; on Nevsky Prospect they would have charged seventy-five roubles for the work alone.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Akaky Akakievich did not want to discuss this with Petrovich, and was afraid of all the large sums with which Petrovich liked to throw dust in people's eyes. He paid him, thanked him and went straight out in the new overcoat to the department. Petrovich went out after him and, remaining in the street, for a long time still looked from afar at the overcoat, and then went purposely aside, so that, going round by a crooked lane, he could run back into the street and look once more at his overcoat from the other side, that is, straight in the face. Meanwhile Akaky Akakievich walked in the most festive disposition of all his senses. He felt every moment of every minute that he had a new overcoat on his shoulders, and several times even smiled with inward pleasure. In truth there were two advantages: one that it was warm, the other that it was handsome.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He did not notice the road at all and found himself suddenly in the department; in the porter's lodge he took off the overcoat, looked it over all round and entrusted it to the special care of the porter. How it happened is not known, but in the department everybody suddenly learned that Akaky Akakievich had a new overcoat and that the dressing gown no longer existed. Everyone in that same minute ran out into the porter's lodge to look at Akaky Akakievich's new overcoat. They began to congratulate him, to greet him, so that at first he only smiled, and then he even felt ashamed. And when everyone, crowding round him, began to say that the new overcoat must be christened, and that at the very least he must give them all an evening, Akaky Akakievich was completely lost, did not know what to do, what to answer and how to excuse himself.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: A few minutes later, all flushed, he began to assure them, rather simple-heartedly, that it was not a new overcoat at all, that it was nothing, that it was an old overcoat. At last one of the clerks, even some assistant to a head of section, probably in order to show that he was not in the least proud and associated even with those beneath him, said:

speaker: MINOR
text: “So be it, I give the evening instead of Akaky Akakievich and invite you all to tea at my place today: as it happens, it is my name day today.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The clerks, naturally, at once congratulated the assistant head of section and accepted the invitation willingly. Akaky Akakievich began to decline, but they all began to say that it was discourteous, that it was simply a shame and a disgrace, and he could in no way refuse. Afterwards, however, he felt pleased when he remembered that he would thereby have an occasion to walk out even in the evening in the new overcoat.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: That whole day was for Akaky Akakievich like the greatest solemn holiday. He returned home in the happiest state of mind, took off the overcoat and hung it carefully on the wall, admiring once more the cloth and the lining, and then purposely pulled out, for comparison, his former dressing gown, quite fallen to pieces. He looked at it and even laughed himself: such a distant difference! And for a long time afterwards at dinner he kept smiling whenever the condition of the old garment came into his mind. He dined cheerfully and after dinner wrote nothing, no papers at all, but lounged a little on his bed until it grew dark. Then, not dragging the matter out, he dressed, put the overcoat on his shoulders and went out into the street.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Where exactly the clerk who had invited him lived, unfortunately, we cannot say: our memory begins to fail us badly, and everything there is in Petersburg, all the streets and houses, have so merged and mixed in our head that it is very hard to get anything out of it in good order. However that may be, at least this is certain, that the clerk lived in the better part of the town, and therefore very far from Akaky Akakievich. At first Akaky Akakievich had to pass through some deserted streets with meagre lighting, but as he approached the clerk's flat the streets became livelier, more populous and brighter lit.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Pedestrians began to flash by more often, ladies too, handsomely dressed, began to appear, and men with beaver collars; cabmen with their wooden lattice sleighs studded with gilt nails were met more rarely; on the contrary, there were smart drivers in crimson velvet caps, with lacquered sleighs and bear rugs, and carriages with decorated boxes flew along the street, their wheels squealing on the snow. Akaky Akakievich looked at all this as at a novelty. For several years he had not gone out in the evening. He stopped with curiosity before the lighted window of a shop to look at a picture in which some beautiful woman was shown taking off her shoe, thus baring her whole leg, a very shapely one; while behind her back, from the door of another room, a man with whiskers and a handsome little beard under his lip thrust out his head. Akaky Akakievich shook his head and smiled, and then went on his way.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Why he smiled, whether because he had come across something quite unfamiliar but about which, all the same, everyone retains some sort of instinct, or because he thought, like many other clerks, the following:

speaker: AKAKY
text: “Well, those French! What is there to say, if they want something, then it is certainly...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Or perhaps he did not even think that, for one cannot climb into a man's soul and find out everything he thinks. At last he reached the house where the assistant head of section lived. The assistant head of section lived on a grand scale: a lantern shone on the staircase, the flat was on the second floor. Going into the hall, Akaky Akakievich saw on the floor whole rows of galoshes. Among them, in the middle of the room, stood a samovar, hissing and sending up clouds of steam.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: On the walls hung overcoats and cloaks, some of them even with beaver collars or velvet lapels. Behind the wall noise and talk could be heard, which suddenly became clear and ringing when the door opened and a footman came out with a tray laden with emptied glasses, a cream jug and a basket of rusks. It was plain that the clerks had long since gathered and had drunk their first glass of tea. Akaky Akakievich, having hung up his overcoat himself, went into the room, and before him there flashed at once candles, clerks, pipes, card tables, and his ear was dimly struck by the quick conversation rising from all sides and the noise of chairs being moved. He stopped very awkwardly in the middle of the room, looking about and trying to think what to do. But they had already noticed him, received him with a shout, and all went at once into the hall and again looked over his overcoat.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Akaky Akakievich, although he was partly abashed, being a sincere man, could not help rejoicing to see everyone praise the overcoat. Then, of course, they all abandoned both him and the overcoat and turned, as usual, to the tables set out for whist. All this, the noise, talk and crowd of people, was somehow wonderful to Akaky Akakievich. He simply did not know what to do, where to put his hands, his feet and his whole figure; at last he sat down beside the players, looked at the cards, peered into one face and another, and after some time began to yawn, to feel bored, the more so since the time at which he usually went to bed had long since come. He wanted to take leave of the host, but they would not let him go, saying that he must by all means drink a glass of champagne in honour of the new garment.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: An hour later supper was served, consisting of vinaigrette salad, cold veal, pâté, pastries and champagne. They made Akaky Akakievich drink two glasses, after which he felt that the room had grown merrier, yet he could not forget that it was already twelve o'clock and that it was long since time to go home. So that the host should not think of detaining him, he went quietly out of the room, found his overcoat in the hall, which he saw, not without regret, lying on the floor, shook it, removed every speck of fluff from it, put it on his shoulders and went down the stairs into the street. In the street it was still light.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Some little shops, those unchanging clubs of house servants and all sorts of people, were open, and others, which were shut, showed all the same a long stream of light along the whole crack of the door, signifying that they were not yet deprived of company and that probably the maids or servants were still finishing their talk and conversation, plunging their masters into complete bewilderment as to their whereabouts. Akaky Akakievich walked in a merry frame of mind, even ran suddenly, he did not know why, after some lady who passed by like lightning and every part of whose body was full of extraordinary motion. But he stopped at once and went on again as before, very quietly, himself marvelling at the trot that had come from he knew not where. Soon there stretched before him those deserted streets which are not cheerful even by day, and still less in the evening.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Now they became still more silent and lonely: the street lamps began to flash by more rarely, for less oil was evidently being allowed; wooden houses and fences began; not a soul anywhere; only the snow sparkled in the streets, and the sleeping low hovels with closed shutters showed black and sad. He approached the place where the street was cut across by an endless square, with houses barely visible on its other side, which looked like a fearful desert.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Far away, God knows where, the light of a fire flickered in some sentry box that seemed to stand at the end of the world. Akaky Akakievich's gaiety here diminished considerably. He stepped onto the square not without some involuntary fear, exactly as if his heart foreboded something evil. He looked back and to the sides: it was exactly like a sea around him.

speaker: AKAKY
text: “No, better not to look,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he thought, and walked on with his eyes shut, and when he opened them to find out whether the end of the square was near, he suddenly saw that before him, almost under his nose, stood some men with moustaches, what sort exactly he could not even make out. His eyes clouded over and his heart pounded.

speaker: MINOR
text: “Why, that overcoat is mine!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said one of them in a voice of thunder, seizing him by the collar. Akaky Akakievich was about to shout “Help!” when the other put a fist the size of a clerk's head right to his mouth, adding:

speaker: MINOR
text: “Just you shout!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Akaky Akakievich felt only that they took the overcoat off him, gave him a kick with a knee, and he fell on his back in the snow and felt nothing more. After a few minutes he came to himself and got up on his feet, but there was nobody. He felt that it was cold in the open and that the overcoat was gone, began to shout, but his voice, it seemed, had no thought of reaching the ends of the square.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In despair, not ceasing to shout, he set off running across the square straight to the sentry box, beside which stood a watchman who, leaning on his halberd, was looking, it seems, with curiosity, wishing to know what the devil this man was running towards him from afar and shouting for. Akaky Akakievich, running up to him, began in a breathless voice to shout that he was asleep and was not minding anything, did not see how a man was being robbed. The watchman answered that he had seen nothing, that he had seen two men stop him in the middle of the square, but supposed they were his friends; and that, instead of scolding in vain, he had better go to the inspector tomorrow, and the inspector would find out who had taken the overcoat.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Akaky Akakievich ran home in complete disorder: his hair, of which a little still grew at the temples and the back of his head, was quite dishevelled; his side and chest and all his trousers were covered with snow. The old woman, his landlady, hearing a terrible knocking at the door, hastily jumped out of bed and ran to open it with a shoe on one foot only, holding her nightgown to her bosom with her hand out of modesty; but on opening she stepped back, seeing Akaky Akakievich in such a state.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And when he told her what the matter was, she threw up her hands and said that he must go straight to the district superintendent, that the local police officer would cheat him, make promises and lead him a dance; and that best of all was to go straight to the superintendent, that she even knew him, because Anna, the Finnish woman who used to be her cook, was now in service with the superintendent as a nurse; that she often saw him himself driving past their house, and that he also came every Sunday to church, prayed, and at the same time looked cheerfully at everyone, and that therefore, by all signs, he must be a good man. Having heard this decision, Akaky Akakievich plodded sadly to his room, and how he spent the night there is left to be judged by anyone who can in the least imagine another's position.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Early in the morning he set out for the superintendent; but they said he was asleep; he came at ten, they said again: asleep; he came at eleven o'clock, they said: the superintendent is not at home; he came at dinner time, but the clerks in the anteroom would by no means let him in and wanted to know at all costs on what business and what need had brought him and what had happened. So that at last Akaky Akakievich, once in his life, wanted to show character and said flatly that he must see the superintendent himself in person, that they dared not refuse him admittance, that he had come from his department on official business, and that if he complained of them, then they would see. Against this the clerks dared say nothing, and one of them went to call the superintendent. The superintendent received the story of the robbery of the overcoat in an extremely strange way.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Instead of turning his attention to the main point of the case, he began to question Akaky Akakievich: why was he returning so late, and had he not called in at, or been to, some disreputable house, so that Akaky Akakievich was quite abashed and left him, not knowing himself whether the case of the overcoat would take its proper course or not. All that day he was not at the office (the only occasion in his life). The next day he appeared quite pale and in his old dressing gown, which had become still more pitiful. The tale of the robbery of the overcoat, in spite of the fact that there were clerks who did not let even this pass without laughing at Akaky Akakievich, nevertheless touched many.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: They decided on the spot to make a collection for him, but collected the merest trifle, because the clerks had already spent a great deal, subscribing to the director's portrait and to some book, at the suggestion of the head of the department, who was a friend of the author; so the sum turned out the merest trifle. Somebody, moved by compassion, resolved at least to help Akaky Akakievich with good advice, telling him not to go to the local police officer, because although it might happen that the officer, wishing to earn the approval of his superiors, would somehow find the overcoat, the overcoat would nevertheless remain at the police unless he produced legal proof that it belonged to him; but that best of all was to apply to a certain Important Person, that the Important Person, by writing and corresponding with whom it was proper, could make the matter go forward more successfully. There was nothing to be done: Akaky Akakievich resolved to go to the Important Person.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Which post exactly the Important Person held, and in what it consisted, has remained unknown to this day. It must be known that a certain Important Person had only recently become an Important Person, and until that time he had been an unimportant person. Moreover, his position was not even now considered important in comparison with others still more important. But there will always be found such a circle of people for whom what is unimportant in the eyes of others is already important. Besides, he tried to increase his importance by many other means, namely: he arranged that the lower clerks should meet him on the stairs when he came to work; that no one should dare to come to him directly, but that everything should go in the strictest order: a collegiate registrar should report to a provincial secretary, the provincial secretary to a titular councillor or whoever else was appropriate, and only in this way should the matter reach him.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So it is in holy Russia, everything is infected with imitation, everyone mimics and apes his superior. They even say that a certain titular councillor, when he was made head of some small separate chancellery, at once partitioned off a special room for himself, calling it “the Room of Presence,” and posted at the doors some doormen with red collars and gold braid, who took hold of the door handle and opened the door to everyone who came, although in the “Room of Presence” an ordinary writing table could barely be fitted. The manners and customs of the Important Person were solid and majestic, but not complicated. The chief foundation of his system was strictness.

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “Strictness, strictness and strictness,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he used to say, and at the last word he would usually look very significantly into the face of the man he was speaking to. Although, in fact, there was no reason for this, because the dozen clerks who made up the entire governmental mechanism of the chancellery were in due fear in any case: seeing him from afar, they would leave their work and wait standing at attention until the chief had crossed the room. His ordinary conversation with his inferiors smacked of strictness and consisted almost of three phrases:

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “How dare you? Do you know who you are speaking to? Do you understand who is standing before you?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: However, in his heart he was a kind man, good to his colleagues, obliging; but the rank of general had quite turned his head. Having received the rank of general, he somehow became confused, lost his way and did not know at all what to do.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: If it happened that he was with his equals, he was still a man as he ought to be, a very decent man, in many respects not even a stupid man; but as soon as he found himself in company where there were people even one rank lower than he, there he was simply impossible: he kept silent, and his position aroused pity, the more so since he himself even felt that he could have spent the time incomparably better. In his eyes there was sometimes seen a strong desire to join some interesting conversation or circle, but he was stopped by the thought: would it not be too much on his part, would it not be familiar, and would he not lose his dignity by it?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And as a result of such reflections he remained for ever in one and the same silent state, uttering only now and then some monosyllabic sounds, and so earned the title of the most tedious of men. To this very Important Person our Akaky Akakievich presented himself, and presented himself at the most unfavourable time, very inopportunely for himself, though opportunely enough for the Important Person. The Important Person was in his study and had fallen into a very, very cheerful chat with an old acquaintance and childhood friend who had recently arrived and whom he had not seen for several years. At this moment they announced to him that a certain Bashmachkin had come. He asked abruptly:

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “Who is he?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: They answered him:

speaker: MINOR
text: “Some clerk.”

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “Ah! He can wait, this is not the time,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the Important Person.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Here it must be said that the Important Person was telling a complete lie: he had time; he and his friend had long since talked over everything and had long been interspersing their conversation with very long silences, only lightly patting each other on the thigh and saying:

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “So it is, Ivan Abramovich!”

speaker: MINOR
text: “That's how it is, Stepan Varlamovich!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But for all that he ordered the clerk to wait, to show his friend, a man who had long since left the service and settled at home in the country, how long clerks waited in his anteroom. At last, having talked his fill, and still more having been silent his fill, and having smoked a cigar in a very comfortable armchair with a reclining back, he finally seemed suddenly to remember and said to the secretary, who stood at the door with papers for his report:

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “Why, there is a clerk standing there, it seems; tell him he may come in.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Seeing Akaky Akakievich's humble appearance and his old uniform coat, he turned to him suddenly and said:

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “What do you want?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: in an abrupt and firm voice, which he had purposely learned beforehand, alone in his room and before the mirror, a week before receiving his present post and rank of general. Akaky Akakievich had already felt the proper timidity in advance, was somewhat confused, and as best he could, as far as freedom of tongue allowed, explained, adding the particle “you know” even more often than at other times, that the overcoat was quite new, and now he had been robbed in an inhuman manner, and that he was applying to him so that by his intercession he might somehow, you know, correspond with the Chief of Police, or someone else, and find the overcoat. To the general, for some unknown reason, such a manner seemed familiar.

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “What are you about, my dear sir,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he went on abruptly.

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “Do you not know the procedure? Where have you come? Do you not know how business is done? You should first have submitted a petition to the chancellery; it would have gone to the head of section, to the head of the department, then it would have been passed to the secretary, and the secretary would have delivered it to me...”

speaker: AKAKY
text: “But, your Excellency,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Akaky Akakievich, trying to gather the small handful of presence of mind that was in him, and feeling at the same time that he was sweating terribly,

speaker: AKAKY
text: “I presumed to trouble your Excellency because secretaries are, you know... an unreliable people...”

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “What, what, what?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the Important Person.

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “Where did you get such boldness? Where did you get such ideas? What sort of insubordination has spread among young people against their chiefs and superiors!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Important Person, it seems, did not notice that Akaky Akakievich was already past fifty. Therefore, if he could be called a young man at all, it was only relatively, that is, in relation to someone who was already seventy.

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “Do you know to whom you are saying this? Do you understand who is standing before you? Do you understand it, do you understand it? I ask you.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Here he stamped his foot, raising his voice to such a powerful note that even someone other than Akaky Akakievich would have been frightened. Akaky Akakievich simply died away, staggered, trembled in his whole body and could not stand at all: had the porters not run up at once to support him, he would have flopped onto the floor; he was carried out almost motionless. And the Important Person, pleased that the effect had surpassed even his expectation and quite intoxicated by the thought that his word could even deprive a man of his senses, glanced sidelong at his friend to learn how he looked on this, and saw not without satisfaction that his friend was in a most uncertain state and was even beginning on his part to feel fear.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: How he went down the stairs, how he came out into the street, Akaky Akakievich remembered none of this. He felt neither his hands nor his feet. Never in his life had he been so severely dressed down by a general, and a strange one at that. He walked through the blizzard that whistled in the streets, with his mouth open, straying off the pavements; the wind, in the Petersburg manner, blew on him from all four sides, from all the lanes. In an instant a quinsy blew into his throat, and he reached home unable to say a single word; he swelled all over and took to his bed. So strong is sometimes a proper reprimand! The very next day a violent fever showed itself.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Thanks to the generous assistance of the Petersburg climate, the illness went faster than could have been expected, and when the doctor came, after feeling the pulse he found nothing to do but prescribe a poultice, solely so that the patient should not be left without the beneficent help of medicine; and, by the way, he announced to him at once that in a day and a half there would certainly be the end. After which he turned to the landlady and said:

speaker: MINOR
text: “And you, my good woman, do not lose time in vain; order him a pine coffin now, because an oak one would be too dear for him.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Whether Akaky Akakievich heard these words, fatal for him, and if he heard them, whether they had a shattering effect on him, whether he pitied his wretched life, none of this is known, because he was all the time in delirium and fever.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Visions, one stranger than the next, appeared to him incessantly: now he saw Petrovich and ordered him to make an overcoat with some traps for thieves, who kept seeming to him to be under the bed, and he kept calling the landlady to drag one thief even from under his blanket; now he asked why his old dressing gown hung before him when he had a new overcoat; now it seemed to him that he was standing before the general, listening to a proper dressing-down and saying: “I am to blame, your Excellency”; now, finally, he even cursed, uttering the most dreadful words, so that the old landlady crossed herself, never having heard anything of the sort from him in her life, the more so as these words followed directly after the words “your Excellency.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Later he talked complete nonsense, so that nothing could be understood; one could only see that disordered words and thoughts were revolving round one and the same overcoat. At last poor Akaky Akakievich gave up the ghost. Neither his room nor his belongings were sealed, because, in the first place, there were no heirs, and in the second, very little inheritance remained, namely: a bunch of goose quills, a quire of white government paper, three pairs of socks, two or three buttons that had come off his trousers, and the dressing gown already known to the reader. To whom all this went, God knows: about this, I confess, even the teller of this tale did not take an interest. Akaky Akakievich was carried away and buried. And Petersburg was left without Akaky Akakievich, as though he had never been in it.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: There vanished and disappeared a being protected by no one, dear to no one, interesting to no one, who had not even drawn the attention of the naturalist, who never fails to stick a pin through a common fly and examine it under the microscope; a being who bore submissively the jeers of the chancellery and went to his grave without any extraordinary deed, but for whom all the same, though just before the end of his life, there flashed a bright guest in the shape of an overcoat, which brought a moment of life to his poor existence, and on whom afterwards misfortune fell as unbearably as it has fallen on the kings and rulers of the world...

speaker: NARRATOR
text: A few days after his death a porter was sent from the department to his lodging, with an order that he appear at once: the chief demanded him; but the porter had to return with nothing, reporting that he could not come any more, and to the question “Why?” he expressed himself in the words:

speaker: MINOR
text: “Well, he's dead, they buried him four days ago.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In this way the department learned of the death of Akaky Akakievich, and the next day a new clerk was already sitting in his place, much taller, who set down his letters in a handwriting not so upright but far more slanting and askew.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But who could have imagined that this was not yet all about Akaky Akakievich, that he was destined to live noisily for a few days after his death, as if in reward for a life that no one had noticed? But so it happened, and our poor story unexpectedly takes on a fantastic ending. Rumours suddenly spread through Petersburg that near the Kalinkin Bridge and far beyond, a dead man had begun to appear at night in the form of a clerk, searching for some stolen overcoat and, under the pretext of the stolen overcoat, dragging from everyone's shoulders, regardless of rank and title, every kind of overcoat: with cat fur, with beaver, with wadding, raccoon, fox, bear coats, in a word every sort of fur and hide that men have devised to cover their own.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: One of the department's clerks saw the dead man with his own eyes and at once recognised Akaky Akakievich in him; but this inspired in him such terror that he took to his heels and therefore could not make him out properly, and saw only how the figure from afar shook a finger at him. From all sides complaints came in ceaselessly that backs and shoulders, and if only those of titular councillors, but even those of privy councillors themselves, were exposed to a perfect chill because of the nightly dragging off of overcoats. The police were ordered to catch the dead man at all costs, alive or dead, and to punish him in the most severe manner as an example to others, and in this they all but succeeded.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Indeed, a watchman of some district in Kiryushkin Lane had already quite caught the dead man by the collar on the very scene of the crime, in the attempt to pull off the frieze coat of some retired musician who in his day had whistled on the flute. Having seized him by the collar, he summoned with his shout two other comrades, whom he charged to hold him, while he himself reached for just one minute into his boot to pull out from there his snuff horn and refresh for a time his nose, which had been frostbitten six times in his life; but the snuff must have been of the kind that even a dead man could not bear. The watchman had no sooner, closing his right nostril with a finger, drawn in half a handful with the left, than the dead man sneezed so violently that he quite splashed the eyes of all three.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: While they raised their fists to wipe them, the dead man's trace vanished, so that they did not even know whether he had really been in their hands. From that time watchmen conceived such a fear of the dead that they were afraid even to seize the living, and only shouted from afar,

speaker: MINOR
text: “Hey, you, go your own way!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: and the dead clerk began to appear even beyond the Kalinkin Bridge, causing no small terror among all timid people. But we have quite abandoned a certain Important Person, who in truth was almost the cause of the fantastic turn of this otherwise perfectly true history. First of all, the duty of justice requires it to be said that the Important Person, soon after the departure of poor Akaky Akakievich, dressed down to shreds, felt something like regret. Compassion was not foreign to him; his heart was open to many good impulses, in spite of the fact that rank very often prevented them from showing themselves.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: As soon as his visiting friend had left his study, he even fell to thinking about poor Akaky Akakievich. And from that time almost every day the pale Akaky Akakievich, who had not withstood the official reprimand, appeared before him. The thought of him troubled him to such a degree that a week later he resolved even to send a clerk to him to find out how he was and whether he could really help him in some way; and when they reported to him that Akaky Akakievich had died suddenly of a fever, he was even struck, heard the reproaches of conscience, and was out of sorts all day.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Wishing to distract himself somewhat and forget the unpleasant impression, he went to an evening party at the house of one of his friends, where he found respectable company, and what was best of all, everyone there was almost of the same rank, so that he could not be constrained by anything. This had a wonderful effect on his state of mind. He unbent, became pleasant in conversation, amiable; in a word, he spent the evening very agreeably. At supper he drank a couple of glasses of champagne, a remedy which, as is well known, works not badly in the matter of merriment. The champagne gave him a taste for various extraordinary things, namely: he decided not to go home yet, but to call on a lady of his acquaintance, Karolina Ivanovna, a lady, it seems, of German origin, to whom he felt quite friendly relations. It must be said that the Important Person was no longer a young man, a good husband, a respectable father of a family.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Two sons, one of whom already served in a chancellery, and a pretty sixteen-year-old daughter with a somewhat curved but charming little nose, came every day to kiss his hand, saying:

speaker: WOMAN
text: “Bonjour, papa.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: His wife, still a fresh woman and not at all bad-looking, would first let him kiss her hand, and then, turning it over to the other side, kiss his hand. But the Important Person, though quite content with the tenderness of his family life, found it proper to have, for friendly relations, a lady friend in another part of the town. This lady friend was not a bit better or younger than his wife; but such puzzles exist in the world, and it is not our business to judge them.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So the Important Person went down the stairs, got into his sleigh and said to the coachman:

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “To Karolina Ivanovna's,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: and himself, wrapping himself very luxuriously in a warm overcoat, remained in that pleasant state than which a Russian can imagine none better, that is, when you think of nothing yourself and meanwhile thoughts creep into your head of their own accord, each more pleasant than the last, not even giving you the trouble of chasing or seeking them. Full of satisfaction, he lightly recalled all the merry moments of the evening he had spent, all the words that had made the small circle roar with laughter; many of them he even repeated in an undertone and found that they were as funny as before, and therefore it was no wonder that he himself chuckled heartily.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: From time to time, however, he was disturbed by a gusty wind which, bursting out suddenly, God knows from where and for what reason, cut right into his face, flinging scraps of snow into it, bellying out his overcoat collar like a sail, or suddenly with unnatural force throwing it over his head and thus causing him endless trouble to scramble out of it. Suddenly the Important Person felt that someone had caught him very tightly by the collar. Turning round, he noticed a man of small stature in an old, worn uniform coat, and not without horror recognised in him Akaky Akakievich. The clerk's face was white as snow and looked quite like a dead man's.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But the horror of the Important Person surpassed all bounds when he saw the dead man's mouth twist and, breathing on him a terrible smell of the grave, utter these words:

speaker: GHOST
text: “Ah! So here you are at last! At last I have, you know, caught you by the collar! It is your overcoat that I need! You did not bestir yourself about mine, and on top of that you gave me a dressing-down. Now hand over your own!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The poor Important Person nearly died. However strong his character might be in the chancellery and generally before his inferiors, and though everyone, looking at his manly bearing and figure alone, would say: “Oh, what a character!” here, like very many who have a heroic exterior, he felt such fear that not without reason he even began to fear some sort of seizure. He himself even threw the overcoat off his shoulders as quickly as he could and cried to the coachman in a voice not his own:

speaker: IMPORTANT PERSON
text: “Drive home at full speed!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The coachman, hearing the voice which is usually uttered at decisive moments and is even accompanied by something much more effective, tucked his head into his shoulders just in case, brandished his whip and dashed off like an arrow. In a little more than six minutes the Important Person was already at his own front door. Pale, frightened and without his overcoat, instead of going to Karolina Ivanovna he came home, dragged himself somehow to his room and spent the night in great disorder, so that the next morning at tea his daughter said to him plainly:

speaker: WOMAN
text: “You are quite pale today, Papa.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But Papa was silent and said not a word to anyone about what had happened to him, and where he had been, and where he had wanted to go. This incident made a strong impression on him.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He even began to say far more rarely to his subordinates: “How dare you, do you understand who is before you”; and if he did say it, it was not until he had first heard what the matter was. But still more remarkable is this, that from that time the appearance of the dead clerk quite ceased: evidently the general's overcoat fitted him perfectly across the shoulders; at least no cases were heard of anywhere of overcoats being dragged off anyone. However, many active and anxious people would not calm down at all and said that in the distant parts of the town the dead clerk was still appearing.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And indeed, one watchman in Kolomna saw with his own eyes a ghost appear from behind a house; but being by nature somewhat feeble, so that once an ordinary full-grown piglet, rushing out of some private house, knocked him off his feet, to the great laughter of the cabmen standing round, from whom he extorted for such mockery a groat apiece for tobacco, so, being feeble, he did not dare to stop it, but followed it in the darkness until at last the ghost suddenly looked round and, stopping, asked:

speaker: GHOST
text: “What do you want?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: and showed such a fist as you will not find even among the living. The watchman said,

speaker: MINOR
text: “Nothing,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: and turned back that same minute. The ghost, however, was by now much taller, wore enormous moustaches, and, directing its steps, as it seemed, towards the Obukhov Bridge, vanished completely in the darkness of the night.
